newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Santander to focus on commercial banking.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Santander to focus on commercial banking.

text.p: Spain's Santander Bank chairman Emilio Botin reaffirmed the group's future focus on commercial banking and said investments in industry would be determined by financial, not strategic, considerations.

Speaking at the annual shareholders meeting at the weekend, Botin stressed the importance of international expansion, particularly the Spanish banking giant's growing penetration of Latin America through purchases of majority stakes.
He said he hopes to double net attributable profits from Latin American investments in 1997.
"Santander has always been much more focused on commercial banking and facing the future, the board has decided to reaffirm and stress this singularity," Botin said.
Botin rejected participation as a core shareholder in companies like Endesa due to incompatability.
"When Santander invests in industry, it does it with a financial motive detached from other considerations of control or management," he said.

Santander realised capital gains of 17 billion pesetas from its sale of an 8.5 percent stake in Spain's second mobile telephone operator Airtel, which reduced its stake to to 5.5 percent, and from the sale of 50 percent of its joint venture with British Telecommunications.
The chairman said those sales were examples of deals which had achieved a critical mass for divestment.

Botin also underscored the potential for commercial banking in the Spanish market through an improvement in its network and the relaunching of commercial activity by subsidiary Banesto in which Santander has a 50 percent stake.
With regard to international expansion, he demonstrated a preference for buying majority stakes in banks.
"With minority stakes...you acquire all the risks but forfeit a large part of the profits which other shareholders get," he said.
In 1996, the group's stake in Latin America brought net attributable profits of $200 million and in 1997, Botin said he expects that figure to double.
Santander has 42 percent of its resources in foreign investments. Of that, 11 percent is in Europe, 14 percent in the U.S. and 17 percent in Latin America.
The company said the market value of investments abroad now stands at $8.451 billion which implies latent capital gains of more than 500 billion pesetas or $3.95 billion.
Foreign investments account for 41 percent of the group's total income. Of that 14 percent comes from Europe, 13 percent from North America and 14 percent from Latin American.

Botin reiterated the group's objectives of an 18-20 percent return on equity in the next three years versus 15.6 percent in 1996 and a minimum compound annual growth for earnings per share of 15 percent versus 13.6 in 1996.
He also expects a reduction in the ratio of operating costs to operating margin to 55 percent from 63 percent last year.
